title: How to Hack Passwords
summary: Looks at password cracking from the attacker's side so that defences make sense: identical hashes reveal shared passwords, hash tables and dictionary attacks reverse weak passwords quickly, GPUs make guessing fast, and only long, non-dictionary passwords resist. Sets up salting as the next fix.

concepts.heading: Context and motivation
points: Hashing passwords already puts a site ahead of many real ones. Sites that can email you your actual password are demonstrably storing it in plain text or reversibly encrypted; a plaintext-offenders listing site collects examples. Delete accounts on such sites; developers can use them as a prompt to offer security help.

Large breaches have exposed millions of accounts, and leaked credentials are traded. Check your own email on a breach-notification service and change any password that appears, everywhere it was reused.

concepts.heading: How a leaked hash table is attacked
points: A hash function is deterministic: the same password always yields the same hash. That is what makes login verification work, and also what lets an attacker spot users who share a password: identical hashes in the leaked table.
Attacker builds a hash table: hash lots of likely passwords (123456, qwerty, password, 111111, ...) with the same function, then look up each stolen hash in the table to read off the password.
Dictionary attack: hash every dictionary word (~150,000), plus phone-number style digits and all character combinations up to about six characters, reaching roughly 20 billion entries.
GPUs compute hashes in parallel; a modern one does around 20 billion MD5 hashes per second, so a table of that size takes about a second. MD5 is especially fast, so pre-built MD5 tables are common.
Pre-built tables exist for the most common passwords, drawn from earlier breaches and annual top-password lists. Pasting a hash into a search engine can even reveal the original.

concepts.heading: What defends a user
points: A strong password's hash will not appear in any table. Cracking cost grows exponentially with length.
Demo with a password strength checker: a 6-character random password falls in seconds on a desktop to brute force; doubling to 12 characters moves it to decades on a desktop and years on a fast GPU.
Length matters more than composition rules; short passwords with a capital and a symbol are still weak.
Avoid dictionary words, place names and anything found in a directory such as phone numbers.
(Extra) Use a password manager so every site gets a unique long random password.

concepts.heading: Developer takeaways
points: Fast, unsalted hashes (MD5) are not enough; the next lesson addresses the table and dictionary problem with salting.
(Extra) Also add rate limiting, breached-password checks and slow password hashes (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2).

pitfalls: Identical hashes in a table expose users sharing a password.
Complexity rules with short length give false confidence.
Only test cracking techniques on your own data; the lesson is educational.

gaps_and_ideas: New lesson 'How passwords get cracked': tasks: (1) hash four common passwords with SHA-256 via crypto.subtle, (2) build a hash-to-password lookup, (3) find which users in a sample leaked table share a password, (4) estimate crack time for lengths 6 vs 12 given guesses per second, (5) list three defences. Interactive demo: paste a hash from a small leaked table and watch a lookup find it, then toggle 'add salt' to show the lookup failing.
